narrative:
The model determined that you have a 90.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and wants students likely to succeed, this strong prediction of failure led directly to the rejection of your application.

Three factors stood out as most important in the decision. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the single biggest reason the model predicted failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of accepted students, who typically rank around the middle of their class. This low ranking strongly pushed the prediction toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 25.5 was the second most influential factor. It sits well below the average of 37 for students who were admitted, pulling the prediction further toward not passing the bar.

Your first-year class ranking came third. Like your third-year rank, you placed in the lowest decile while accepted students average around the sixth decile. This also contributed to the model’s expectation that you would struggle on the bar exam.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your upper-middle family income, 3.0 undergraduate GPA, and plan to attend full-time.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Targeted bar-prep courses or a post-baccalaureate program could also help demonstrate readiness for the exam. Reapply once you have concrete evidence of improvement in these core areas. (248 words)
